Yes. We come here
to one of the most difficult, the most debatable, and most debated npon, questions that governments of all nations have had to deal with in the past. Military authorities in every country have, after various and multiplied experiments, adopted a certain type of boot for their army, but the pattern varies according to the country. The English boot is different from the French and is still more at variance with the American. The American army boot is the lightest by a great deal. As far as weight is concerned, the English boot is the heaviest, then comes the French, the Canadian, and lastly the American. The latter was adopted by the United States army after four years of experiments, and after they had examined the patterns used bj all the great nations of the world.
Consequently, is it possible, or is it fair to cast blame on the Canadian Government, before as well as after 1911, or on the officers of the militia staff, for having pronounced in favour of a boot somewhat lighter than the British boot and somewhat heavier than the American? No; I say it is not. It is a matter of opinion which will always be open to- discussion. It may never be settled absolutely satisfactorily, but if the problem is ever solved it will probably be due to the fact that the means will have been found for giving three pairs of boots to each soldier, one pair of rubber boots for circumstances such as were found 152	.

at Salisbury Plain, one pair of heavy boots for trench work in France, and one pair of light boots (like the Canadian) for marching to Berlin, the quickest possible.
Just now, here in Canada, opinions of experts are divided into three categories: One favours the heavy boot of the standard screw type with hob nails and steel plat-;, like the English one, another lauds the use of the light boot of the Canadian type (Goodyear welt), while others recommend a combination of the two. It is reasonable to think that the British army boot, because of its weight, shrould be more suitable for the new process of underground war and trenches than the light one, but for the same reason, that is because of its weight, ilt seems the more unfit for marching. This is a serious defect when one realizes that in war the facility and promptness with which an army can move and displace itself is one of the essentials of victory. Volumes could be written in favour of the light boot.and also in favour of the heavy one as well. This shows that in such questions it is not possible to adopt absolute rules.
A full discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of the British boot would not be in my line, but I may be permitted to say this much that many experts in Canada are strongly in favor of the light boot. Mr. Matthews, Lieutenant Whitby, Pte. Ross, General Hughes, General MacDonald, Colonel Macdonald, Colonel Brown, Colonel Currie, Major Ranger and many others are in favour of the light boot.
It is true that the minority give great weight to the opinions of General Alderson and Sir George Perley. But this is, after all, indirect evidence which cannot destroy the evidence from soldiers having just come back from Salisbury and testifying, under oath, before the committee, opinions contrary to those given by these two gentlemen. Besides, just as much credit could be given to the opinions expressed by Lieut.-Col. Currie and Major Ranger, who have been at Valcartier, at Salisbury Plains, and are to-day on the firing line in France.
Paul Emile Ranger, of Montreal, an officer whom most of the members for Quebec know, gives, in a long and detailed diary recently published by La Presse of Montreal, a vivid account, day by day, from the 11th February to the 6th March, of the life of our soldiers in the trenches and their conduct in action, recording the gallant deeds which have inscribed on the roll of honor the names of such men as Hardy, Valin, Lacroix, Martin, Deloiup

champs, etc. And one would notice, while reading this account, the unassuming way in which the most heroic deeds are recited, showing the deep conviction, the true soldiery spirit of our men, now in war, and whose gallantry showed them to be the worthy comrades of the trained soldiers of France and England. While speaking of their life in the trenches Major Ranger has a word to say about the accoutrements. Ho mentions that his men have been supplied with English military boots and recalls, as his personal experience, that after one hour and a half walking in the trenches at night, he felt as if his shoes weighed fifty pounds. In his diary of the 4th of March he gives the opinion of his men on the same subject as follows:
Their greatest annoyance comes from their boots. They miss their Canadian boots for the English boots are no good. These last boots take credit for heavy and thick soles, but most of the time the sole is too thick for the uppers and after a few days' wearing gives way entirely.
Besides, they are not waterproof. As a general rule our men prefer the Canadian boots, more soft and better constructed, and X share their opinion.
I can give another testimony which should have as much weight as that of Sir George Perley or General Alderson, and it is the testimony of Private H. E. Parker, as contained	in the following letter

309 South Marks Street,
Fort William, Ont.,
April 1, 1915.
The Hon. the Minister of Militia and Defence, Ottawa, Ont.
Sir,-Having reference to the inquiry regarding quality of boots supplied to the soldiers of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, I have the honour to inform you that I have at present in my possession and still wearing, the pair of regulation boots issued to me at Valcartier during the latter part of August, 1914. These boots have been in continual use since issue to date.
I had been issued with a pair of Imperial service boots, but such were stolen from me before I had an opportunity of using them.

All these things being considered, can we find ourselves at all justified in blaming the Canadian Government or the officers of the militia for having kept the Canadian boots as they were? Let us realize that the time for deliberating and making experiments in this respect had gone; it was too late. We had neither four years nor one, nor even one month, to restudy the matter.
The Canadian people, like all the other colonies, were rising, united, to promptly assist the Mother Country. No one in Canada, then, would fail to see an emergency. Can one imagine the indignation that would have been felt in this House and in this country, if, instead of putting himself immediately in a position to issue boots and other equipment to our soldiers,, General Hughes had taken the attitude of making experiments of all kinds? Action was necessary, and the present Minister of Militia, it cannot be denied, answered with immediate action to the best knowledge and ability that could be had and shown in such an emergency, to rapidly equip the Canadian contingents. When war broke out, the Department of Militia had at their disposal a pattern of boot that had been in use since 1900, or at least since 1904, and as to which no serious complaints had been heard. I think we can safely say that this boot was the result of the experience of the South African war, and it was established that it has given satisfaction ever since. General Macdonald, on pages 211, 221, 213 and 216, said that some boots made according to the sealed sample had been worn by our soldiers in South Africa. Lieut.-Col. MacDonald, on page 236, and General Lessard, page 468, said that boot was thought to be advisable under the circumstances. By doing what they do, those who were responsible for efficiency acted prudently and listened to the voice of sound reason. That is the conclusion I have reached on that point. We have purely and simply applied the rule which in matters of liability is acknowledged as a principle of law all over the world, and according to which he who acts like a prudent, diligent, paterfamilias, who administers and manages his business and

property with the ordinary prudence of a reasonable man, must be held to have done what could be possibly expected of him. That is the principle of law laid down in the Civil Code of Quebec, and I presume it is a principle of law which is common to every civilized country in the world.
The boots issued to the soldiers were made according to samples approved by the Government officers, and were in use by the permanent force in Canada. Out of 180,000 pairs made by the manufacturers,
178,000	pairs have already been issued. Several of the manufacturers who obtained boot contracts, gave their evidence before the committee and all agreed that the material was excellent and the workmanship was good. The inspectors placed by the Government to watch over the making of the boots in the factories themselves assure us of their having done all in their power to rigourously inspect the boots in the then pressing circumstances under which the inspection was taking place, and it is established that, with the exception of a few instances of little importance, the hoots were of good quality and in most cases superior to the sample. This is proven by the witnesses, as well as by the two experts, Mr. Hoar and Mr. Cote, who were unanimously chosen by the committee to make a report on the boots. The inspection no doubt did not cover the whole of the 180,000 pairs, because there were about 14,000 pairs which were sent direct to Valcartier and which, because of the pressing demand and lack of accommodation, had to be delivered to the soldiers without inspection. But there was no time to waste and the Tecruits at Valcartier could not be allowed to go without boots, which unanswerable reason made it necessary to issue a certain quantity without inspection. I quote from the evidence of Lieutenant Colonel Hallick, when questioned on this point, at page 59:
By Mr. Rainville:
Q. When you were pressing for the delivery of the boots, did you attend to the requesting of delivery yourself?-A. Yes.
Q. Did you wire any firms or to the Government to press delivery?-A. I only wired to my chief here at headquarters and told him I was short of boots.
Q. Where they shipped to Valcartier camp? -A. They were sent direct from the manufacturers to me on my demand.
This shows that if the boots were delivered at Valcartier without inspection it was for a very good reason, and there is nothing in it to merit blame for the Government or for the officers of the militia. We must not believe that this absence of inspection,

which the manufacturers could not anticipate in order to make a cheap boot, had an influence on the making of the boots in question. The manufacturers could not expect that any of their boots would escape inspection, and surely they would not have run the risk of making bad boots and having them rejected, in the hope that there might be no inspection. It must be admitted that the absence of inspection did certainly involve the issue of certain boots, which, under normal conditions and under inspection, would have been detected as inferior, and rejected.

Certain hon. gentlemen opposite, with minds strongly bent on criticising, hold the Government liable as for a crime for the least omission of any kind. The present Administration and Militia Department will not pretend to possess supernatural infallibility. We maintain that from the evidence adduced, it is clean- that the representatives of the Government, such as superior officers and inspectors, and the manufacturers and fanners, have shown the best of good faith, sincere honesty and great care for the welfare of our soldiers It is possible "that a' few errors of judgment may have occurred on their part; but in all justice must we not give to the Administration, at the head of a country which for more than a hundred years has lived in peace and only in anticipation of a lasting peace, credit for the superhuman efforts made by it in a time of great emergency to face the immediate eventualities of a war which took by surprise all the European countries, except perhaps Germany, which caused it, and which I -hope will get the worst of it?
In this inquiry the attention of the public is centred on the boot question, with no reference made and no regard paid to the innumerable difficulties with which the Administration has had to cope in undertaking to equip with boots, necessary clothes, arms, ammunition, food, and so on, an army of infantry, cavalry and artillery of over 100,000 men. We are within the facts as revealed by the evidence when we assert that the great majority of the boots which were returned to Ottawa as defective had been worn by the soldiers for from six to eight weeks, and we are told by the experts that such is about the limit of time within which a boot may be reasonably expected to wear under the exceptional circumstances which, the inquiry revealed, existed at the time at Val-eartier and in other parts of the country. To prove that, I could quote Lieut.-Col. Hallick at page 59, Mr. Stephens at page 43, and Mr. Silver at pages 305 to 306. A great many of these boots were repairable, but they were not repaired, either through carelessness or through there being no cobblers with the regiments. That, however, is not a good ground on which to hold the Department of Militia or the Government liable for negligence or carelessness or any fault, because it must be observed that the boots which were reported as defective or bad were recently examined by two abso-

Hon. gentlemen opposite attach a great deal of importance to complaints lodged by the local boards of inquiry composed of the officers of various regiments throughout the country. It was objected that a great part of the evidence was not given under oath, and that it had to a great extent no legal value. I do not intend entering here into a discussion -of that question, which has been dealt with fully by my colleagues; I rely only on the reports and on the evidence adduced upon their contents by the officers of these local boards of inquiry who appeared before us to give evidence on the worst cases mentioned in their reports. Without attacking the honour of our soldiers or officers, I wish to express my opinion that these reports do not conclusively establish that the boots so reported defective were all or in the majority of cases defective. I base that opinion on the fact that such inquiries were somewhat hurriedly held and quickly disposed of, and on the lack of experience of those who held them. I may be permitted to add, without offending my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), who often objected in committee when we were trying to find out the reason for the condemnation of the boots, that boards of inquiry were held, in the majority of cases, not with a view to searching into the causes of deterioration of the boots complained of, but in OTder to obtain, through what appeared to be the only available machinery, a second issue of boots. The holding of such boards where boots are to be condemned, is the only means that the regiments have at their disposal to get from the department what they claim from their officers. Let me quote the evidence of Major McKenzie on page 391, as follows:
Our idea was to get these boots condemned so that we could take over our men on parade with decent hoots.
Colonel Jones' evidence on page 345 is as follows:	,
Q. Is it not generally conceded in many regiments that the men want to get new boots as often as they can?-A. Oh. yes.
The reports of these boards are more often rejected than accepted by the department, according to Quartermaster

General Macdonald, and I am under the impression that Major General Fiset said that he had not much confidence in these boards, and that in the Militia Department they were putting them aside because experience showed that they were of little value. A salient fact is that no mention can be found in these reports of any boots that were repairable that may have been burned or cut or destroyed by the wearer. The evidence, however, shows that a certain number of boots deteriorated in that way, and that the great majority of the others were repairable. Let me refer again to the summary of the report of the two experts who examined the condemned boots. Out of 1,713 inspections, only 265 boots were found not worth repairing, and out of these 265, were 112 injured by burning.
What is the reason for that omission? It is to be found in the fact that no deteriorated boot will be renewed which has become defective through fault or negligence of the wearer and he has to get, according to regulations, a new pair at his own expense. A new issue at the public expense will only take place when it is shown that the boots were worn through "fair wear and tear or when they are defective or of bad quality.
Far be from me the idea of trying to blame the officers of the regiments for that zeal towards their soldiers. Nobody would think of blaming them. We are in this war not to try to economize on a few pairs of boots to be supplied to the soldiers, when the loyal soldiers are willing to give their very lives for the welfare and security of the country. We would equally refuse to blame the Department of Militia for accepting boots in the first rush contracts without inspection, when we find the goods furnished by the manufacturers were made according to a sample constructed under the specifications that had been approved since the South African war and discussed many times since.

I would be prepared to say that the Canadian boot, bettered as much as can be through the experience obtained during this war, was very good. Since December the double sole was added, hobnails and horseshoe plates could be added as well to improve the wearing quality of the sole. As a whole the boots have given satisfaction and are the most suitable shoe for our voluntary soldiers. The soldiers themselves are the ones that we .should please and satisfy in general.
Major Ranger and Colonel Currie, at the front, speaking for themselves and for their men, prefer the Canadian boot to the heavy English boot. Witnesses who came back from Salisbury Plain having worn the English boot are of the same opinion, and this is the only direct evidence we had on the question of a heavy boot or a medium boot such as the Canadian.
As far as our Canadian manufacturers are concerned, it is just that out of this inquiry there should come the true con-

The Government had a little more than a month from the time of the first issue of boots to the time when the second order was given, which was ample, in my judgment, for it to have rectified anything that might have been wrong in the boots.

The hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) has referred the members of this House to the evidence produced before the committee which is on record. With even greater confidence I also refer the members of the House to the sworn evidence which is on record, because I be-

lieve it will convince any one with an unbiased mind that the majority report of the committee is founded on fact and cannot be controverted in any essential detail.
All who are interested in public affairs should be anxious in every way possible to discourage dishonest public dealings. In this, it appears to me, there are two attitudes to be avoided; first, that of condoning shady transactions; and, second, of almost equal importance, (that of condemning honest transactions.	-
At the present time, and in the present circumstances, in considering the question of the supply of boots to the Canadian Militia Department, we should exercise an impartial, sane and deliberate judgment based entirely upon facts.
We must remember that criticism of army footwear is as old as war itself. Each campaign by a belligerent country is fought under conditions differing from those of its predecessors, so that after the termination of each campaign each belligerent country naturally reviews the experience of that campaign and ascertains in what ways its boots and other war equipment can be improved. The result is that there is constant change and difference of opinion.
The speakers who have preceded me this afternoon have pointed out that the question of army footwear has occupied the attention of the best minds in the United States, and that an experienced army board there required four years in which to make up its mind as to the best form	of	boot to be	recommended.
It is only within the last week that, in reading trade journals published in the United States, I find that there is an opinion in the trade there that these findings, although made as late as 1912, have already become obsolete, and that there should be now a change in their army boot.
The hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) quoted the evidence of a Canadian manufacturer to the effect that the Canadian Militia Department could easily have made a change from the present specification and ordered different boots within a week. I think I need only point out to him-for he is a man well endowed with discretion-that if the expert American Army Board required four years in which to gather sufficient information to form the basis for an opinion, any suggestion of an interested manufacturer in Canada that a new sample could be supplied and a new specification adopted in a week, is not one that should carry weight with him.
If the hon. gentleman will change that and, instead of saying that they required that time, will say that they took it, I will agree with him.

My hon. friend has had a good deal of experience with and ample opportunity to observe our good neighbours to the south, and I think he will be the last to accuse them of any lack of celerity in their movements, or question their sound business judgment.
The interests involved in the present inquiry are two.
The first is the soldier's comfort, and in that is bound -up the question of national protection. No interest which can be put forward is entitled to as much consideration as this.
But only secondary to that is the interest of an important Canadian industry, one which employs directly 23,000 operatives, and which has, in addition, a large number of shareholders. There are at least 23,000 operatives engaged directly in the Canadian boot manufacturing industry, tanning and leather trades. Using the usual basis of computation of five to a family, we find that over 100,000 of the Canadian population are dependent on this great industry. That is an interest which can be considered only secondary to that of the comfort of the soldiers themselves.
There has been, I regret to say, very noticeable in the discussion and consideration of the supply of boots to the Canadian army, a tendency to condemn without investigation. The press and pulpit have leaped at conclusions with insufficient evidence. I fully appreciate that, because my own views had, before I had any official knowledge or investigation, been influenced both by the press and by the pulpit; for I have read one and have listened to the other.
It seems to me that the obligation of members at the present time is to divest themselves entirely of all the original prejudice which may have been created by these or other influences. Evidence should be gathered from the whole field. It is not safe, it is not advisable, to select isolated bits of evidence, casual statements by witnesses who appeared before the committee. The evidence should be taken as a whole. If any one will take the trouble to read through these twenty-six volumes they will be able to form a pretty accurate judgment. I am afraid even though recom-

mended to members of this House, that course will not be generally followed.
But, more than that, I think that any person who wishes to arrive at a judgment with regard to any matter such as this, is better equipped to do so if he were present and heard personally the evidence given by the different witnesses.
I know that it is superfluous to appeal to hon. members of the House for a careful consideration of the facts and of the evidence. I trust and I believe that every person who has the opportunity of serving his country by occupying a seat in this House will not fail to place the best interest of the country and its national prosperity above party and will render a decision on the facts as on record and not on any preconceived idea or any question that has to do with party advantage or interest.

Mr. McCURDY (resuming): Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) agrees with the report of the committee to the effect that the contracts have been substantially fulfilled by the manufacturers. These reports, I trust, will dispose of the statements which have been going around in the press and which have interfered not a little with the shoe manufacturing industry in Canada. It has been semi-officially stated that substantial contracts from belligerent countries have been cancelled owing to statements made in the press as to the failure of Canadian contractors to carry out their contracts with the department.
The investigation which has been conducted by your committee has been most thorough in all its details. A number of members of this House have occasionally attended that committee, and I am sure their observations will bear out this statement, that nothing in the way of evidence has been ruled out on a technicality, but that, on the contrary, all the rules of evidence, and the practice of previous committees, have been strained to allow anything that in any way could throw light on the matter of boot contracts to 'be admitted.
Naturally I regret the failure of the committee to arrive at a unanimous report. "Unanimity was, I think, particularly desirable at the present time, affecting a question with which is involved that of national defence. The cordial and harmonious relations of members of the committee throughout the investigation seemed to promise, to the uninitiated at any rate, a unanimous report. But other counsels prevailed and we have not a unanimous report, but a report of the majority and a report of the minority, the latter, I feel, not warranted by a fair consideration of the evidence.
It is, however, gratifying that all agree on the essential part, and this gives the lie to the lurid press and pulpit utterances of paper soles and all other fraudulent suggestions-all agree that the boots supplied have been manufactured honestly and in accordance with the contracts.
Furthermore, it has been shown by the investigation that the profits of manufacturers have in all cases been very moderate. The largest manufacturers whom we have had before us and, therefore, presumably the manufacturers best qualified to manufacture at a low cost, testified (see 978 and 980) that the net factory cost, including factory overhead of the boots manufactured at the largest factory, that of the Ames-Holden Company, amounted to $3.39 per pair. They also stated that the overhead expenses of that factory amounted to 19.,02 per cent of the selling price, which would be approximately 63 cents per pair. That overhead expense includes audit, advertising, allowances, cartage, donations, insurance, law costs, light, heat and power branches, office sundries, wages (branches), travelling expenses, rent of branches, taxes, stationery, discount, bank interest, repairs, and bad debts, but does not include interest on capital. This will bring the total cost over $3.85, so they appear to have been manufactured and supplied to the Government without any actual profit to the manufacturer. It is also fair to state that one manufacturer alone said befoie the committee that, even after paying what he called his selling expenses, >a profit remained to the manufacturer of 25 cents per pair. But on the occasion when he next appeared before the committee he gave evidence to the effect that his profits were less than 13 cents a. pair, and he furthermore, I am informed, made statements not in his evidence to the effect that there was an actual loss on the contract. I think T? is a fair statement to make that in no case were any profits of any substantial size made on these contracts.

As to the evidence which has been offered to the committee, my hon. friend from North Oxford has told the House of his personal efforts to investigate. I think all members of the committee have taken pains to go outside the committee room, wherever occasion offered, to observe the condition of the boots on soldiers' feet in actual service, and informal conversations with soldiers and all other means available were employed by the different members of the committee in order to widen the information available.
Reference has been made by every speaker who has preceded me to the regimental boards of inquiry. When the evidence obtained by these regimental boards at the different headquarters first came to my attention, I was of the opinion that the evidence of these boards should be admitted; but it was otherwise decided by the committee. Five members of the committee were leading barristers, and we also had the benefit of counsel, and so six learned barristers decided, probably correctly, that they were not admissible as evidence, for the same reason as the findings of the departmental board of inquiry, sometimes known as the Hallick Board, was not admitted. The principal reason why this was not admitted was that the witnesses had not been sworn; and as the evidence had not been given under oath it was thought by a majority of the committee that the testimony taken before these regimental boards and the Hallick Board should not be received as evidence. Furthermore, with regard to the departmental board, there was always a temptation from being interested, which would be difficult for any departmental officer to fully avoid.
Regimental boards, are held at each of the different divisional headquarters and regimental headquarters of the troops. When new boots were required for any reason by the soldiers, as was explained in evidence, the only way in which these boots could be obtained was through a regimental board. If the regimental board appointed under the authority of the colonel of the .regiment condemned the boots for any other reason than ordinary wear and tear, soldiers could not obtain new boots unless they paid for them themseives.
The function of the regimental boards, therefore, can perhaps be properly stated to be the condemnation of boots. I am

sure that all can understand the temptation to which the officers were subjected to approve of the applications made Dy their soldiers for new footwear. If the board found the boots to be no longer useful on account of fair wear and tear, they recommended that the boots be replaced at the public expense. If the boots were rendered unwearable for other reasons they had to be replaced at the soldier's expense. It is only natural that an officer should try to meet the wishes of his men as far as possible, and if possible, confirm the applications that their soldiers had made.
We made inquiry of the regular departmental officers at Ottawa, and examined among others the director of clothing and equipment, who has particular charge of all the outfits for the men. We wished to ascertain whether he accepted the findings of these regimental boards as final. His evidence is to be found on page 232:
Q. You do not accept the recommendations at all?

A. No.
Q. As a matter of fact you regard them with suspicion?-A. I am afraid we do.
Q. They have been more often rejected than acted upon? A. Yes.
Q. In other words it is the natural desire of the men to get new boots as often as they can?

A. Just so.
Furthermore, it should be remembered that those who gave evidence before these boards, and the members of the boards themselves, were not experts in equipment and their examination of the boots was often casual. The hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) made a good deal of the findings of these boards this afternoon. As I have already stated, their findings were not admitted in the evidence for the reason that those who appeared before the boards as witnesses were not sworn.
But there was also another reason.
When the majority of the members of the committee decided that we could not accept the evidence taken before these regimental boards we scanned the evidence very carefully and summoned before the committee twenty-six witnesses, I think it was, whose evidence in regard to the service given by the boots was the most unfavourable taken by all these regimental boards. These witnesses came before us and gave evidence under oath; but even here we were at a disadvantage for it was only natural that these men should, for the sake of being consistent, seek to uphold in their evidence before the committee the statements they had already made before the regimental board.

As a matter of fact, as subsequent events proved, these regimental boards discharged with a vengeance the functions for which they were created. I have already quoted the evidence of the director of clothing and equipment who said that he always regards the findings of these boards with suspicion, and more often rejects than accepts them. The result of our examination of the -witnesses who had appeared before these regimental boards was exactly what was to be expected. It proved the statements made before the regimental boards to be palpably absurd.
The hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) referred this afternoon to the case of nine pairs of boots which came before the committee from the 7th Artillery Brigade of Ottawa. This regimental board happened to be called towards the end of the Special Committee's sittings, and when its finding came to our attention we asked that the boots be sent to the committee, and that Lieutenant Patterson and Captain McParland appear (to give evidence. It developed in the course of the evidence that of these nine pairs which had been condemned by that regimental board out of a total issue of 267 pairs, two pairs- and this is the evidence of my own senses, for I saw the boots myself; and I am confirmed by the opinion of the committee's experts-were actually wearable at the time1 they appeared before the committee, and our boot expert naturally asked the question: " Why are these boots condemned? That boot as it stands to-day is perfectly wearable." Three other pairs out of the nine were perfectly repairable, and only required the services of a regimental cobbler to be made right again.
Probably the one reason which more than any other contributed to the dissatisfaction with the boots of the troops at the different quarters was that they could only be served with one pair of boots to wear, rain or shine, day or night.
I am not going to quote at any great length from the evidence given by witnesses who appeared before the committee, but we had another officer, Lieutenant Underwood, who came from the Winnipeg division. This man gave evidence before a departmental board held at the agricultural college barracks in the city of Winnipeg
on the 11th January, 1915, and this is his story there as we have it from a perusal of the report of their regimental board:
I have taken at haphazard a number of pairs of boots of the first issue, which were returned to Q.M. stores, and on cutting them open found them composed of "paper, wood, cork and leather scrap, ground and mixed with glue." The uppers of inferior quality, and in my opinion, unfit for active service.
That officer was brought before the committee, and he admitted that it was news to him that in the manufacture of boots ground cork and camenit are recognized as the best filling for Goodyear welt boots, and are required by the specifications of the department. Yet that is his evidence.
The hon. member for Russell this afternoon quoted the evidence of two soldiers only who preferred the British boot to the Canadian boot. We had before us five or six Canadians who enlisted and who saw service at Salisbury Plain. The only members of the Canadian force available to us were asked to appear before the committee and give evidence, and they were unanimous in declaring that they preferred the Canadian boot to the British boot. The opinion of these six men, to my mind, far overruled the opinion of the two privates, McGarvie and Ewing, who were quoted by the hon. member for Russell this afternoon. So far as opinions go with reference to the quality of the boots, the committee, I think very wisely, put their reliance on a committee of experts. After careful deliberation and a good dealof consideration extending over ten days, the committee unanimously decided to select Mr. John A. Hoar, of Halifax, a large custom boot maker, of 30 years experience who had made boots for Imperial officers and soldiers, for naval officers and for the general custom trade, and Mr. Magloire *Cote of St. Hyacinthe, who also has large experience from his youth up in boot making, to assist them in an expert way. These two men, I understand, are one on either side of politics. They were unanimously appointed by the committee and, as I say, I think, the committee wisely decided to commit to them thfe investigation of the condition of the boots which had come to the committee for examination. Their figures have been given to the House a number of times this afternoon, but perhaps they will bear repeating. Immediately on the assembling of the committee, telegrams were sent to all the regimental headquarters
\

throughout the country asking them to send all rejected boots to Ottawa so that the committee could pass upon them definitely. As a result of these directions 1,713 pairs of boots were sentt to the committee as being boots condemned after fair wear and tear by regimental boards. I have previously referred to the findings of these boards as being such as perhaps should not be regarded as conclusive. This opinion has been very much fortified by the developments which have occurred and by the examination of these boots by our experts. They reported that 1,448 oult of the 1,713 condemned hoots were repairable. They reported further that 112 pairs of these boots had been burned. Every one knows that the burning of boots is not destruction by fair wear and tear. The regimental boards said not a word, any of them, about burning, but burnt they were. Therefore, you have conclusive evidence that the findings of these regimental boards are not such as should be depended upon. There were 22 cut by knife and spur and 48 cut by nails. Out of a total lot we will put those cut by nails in the class of boots unrepairable and destroyed by wear and tear and then we have left only .131 out of the 1,713 sent here for inspection, which shows that the regimental boards were wrong in their decisions in 92 cases out of every 100, and right in only 8 cases out of 100. Surely these results justify the decision of the. committee not to accept the findings of the regimental boards as evidence and I am rather surprised that in this discussion my hon. friends opposite should have referred time and time again to the findings of these boards which have been already discarded.
The experience of quite a number of soldiers at Salisbury Plain was given in person to the committee, and I submit that the same rules of evidence should apply to the Salisbury boards as was applied to the regimental boards in Canada. In view of what we found in regard to the credibility of evidence given oefore the Canadian regimental boards, and the developments which have occurred since we examined the witnesses,, considerable reserve should be maintained in regard to these Salisbury boards. Those who gave evidence before the Salisbury boards were almost all, without exception, not sworn. Furthermore, all the soldiers who had experience at Salisbury Plain, without any exception whatever, on coming before our committee testified in the most emphatic manner that they would not wear the

English boots but that they preferred the Canadian boots. The hon. member for Bnuville (Mr. Lemiaux) this afternoon, was very insistent on having the letters received from General Alderson, who was in charge of the Canadian force at Salis-busy, read to the House. Whatever Gen-Alderson's opinion may be, it was necessarily based largely, as were the findings of the regimental boards in Canada, on evidence submitted to him and he would not necessarily express his own opinion nor could he state of his own personal knowledge; but he would give a report based on evidence which was sent up to him by those in authority under him.
We all know that every country has its own particular customs, and every good citizen of a country loves the customs of his country and is prepared to stand by them. We, as good Canadians, prefer Canadian things, and the people of Great Britain, as good Britishers, prefer British things, and it should be borne in mind in considering the expression of General Aider-son as well as the evidence of Mr. McGar-vie and Mr. Ewing, who preferred the British boot, that they have been accustomed to the British boots from their youth up, and that they would naturally favour them.
I shall now deal for a few minutes with the unfair features, as I regard them, of the minority report.
I have already stated that in my innocence, on going into this committee first, I really hoped for a unanimous finding. I went into the committee to consider this question at first under the impression, on account of the utterances in pulpit and press, that a great wrong had been done. I felt very strongly that all evidence possible that could throw light on the subject should be admitted, and I state now that after full consideration of the evidence I am prepared to stand by the report submitted by the committee as being a fair report, and a report warranted by the facts in their widest sense. If the minority report contains unfair features, and many un fair features, it is perhaps because of the fact that certain members have gone into that committee from, the very start to if possible report something unfavourable to and tending to reflect on the Government. I went into that committee with no such intention; I went there with no other intention but to give my verdict exactly according to the evidence. As a sample of what I c insider unfair findings, I shall read from page 599 of the Votes and Pro-

ceedings, paragraphs 43 and 44 of the minority report:
Thirteen hundred and sixty-five pairs of boots, and three hundred and forty-eight odd boots out of the number condemned by the various boards throughout the country were submitted to the inspection of Messrs John A. Hoar, of Halifax, and Magloire C6tS of St. Hyacinthe, who made report thereon, as follows:
That out of said number of boots, two hundred and sixty-five pairs were not worth repairing ; fourteen hundred and forty-eight were repairable, and that sixty-eight boots were not originally equal to the sample. If the proportion of boots in this particular lot, not equal to sample, is a fair percentage of the number of boots furnished that did not come up to sample, out of the one hundred and eighty thousand pairs supplied, the number of boots so furnished that were inferior to sample would be seven thousand two hundred and ninety-eight boots.
If that second paragraph of the minority report which I have read means anything, it means that Mr. John A. Hoar and Mr. Cote found:
If the proportion of boots in this particular lot, not equal to sample, is a fair percentage of the number of boots furnished that did not fome up to sample, out of the one hundred and eighty thousand pairs supplied, the number of boots so furnished that were inferior to sample would be seven thousand two hundred and ninety-eight boots.
As a matter of fact, Messrs. Hoar and Cote found nothing of the kind, and the wording of that paragraph must create a most erroneous impression upon the mind of any reader. To my mind, and I think to the mind of any impartial man who reads it, it is intended to convey an entirely wrong impression as to the finding of these two gentlemen who were appointed a.s experts by the committee. The first sentence alone of the paragraph, not the second or last, is that of Messrs. Hoar and Cote. And ithe representation is the more unfair because these boots are the "dregs" of the whole issues, and thus inevitably yield a larger proportion of bad boots than those not condemned.
Reference has been made to the evidence of Mr. Alfred Minister of Toronto, and is regarded as of so much importance by the minority of the committee that it occupies a whole paragraph in their report. It is stated in this minority report that Mr. Minister would not make shoes according to the sample, knowing that they were to be used by men going on active service, and the impression is conveyed that " he did not want to make any money out of a man's life." Citations from the evidence of Mr. Minister have been made by the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro), 153
and any person who reads that evidence in its entirety will recognize at once that it is most contradictory, and that it destroys the point which the minority report seeks to make out of it. In my opinion, too great weight ought not to be attached to the evidence of this man. His evidence, in the first place, was intended to tmake it appear that because of his high sense of public duty he was willing to forego profits which he might have made, because he did not want to take advantage of the situation. But he was obliged to admit before the committee, first that he would make the selfsame boots if he got his price of $4.65, and, second, that he took no further steps whatever to notify the Government or those responsible of Ithe ideas he expresses at this date of defects; that he sent no word to the Minister of Militia or to his member of Parliament as to his views on the subject. .
Another paragraph in the minority report which cannot fail to attract the attention of any one who has followed the evidence carefully, is piaragraph 21, which is to be found at page 596 of the Votes and Proceedings and which says:
That on October 24th the department directed a change to he made In the sample boot by doing away with the slip sole that had been in use and providing in its place a double sole running through to the back of the heel, but made no further changes in the specifications-
It is correct so far, but listen to this:
-or iin the direction of providing a proper boot for active service.
If anything has been shown by the investigation as regards boots, it is that the trouble is on account of the soles wearing out. A large number of boots have been displayed before the committee; and in almost all the cases, the difficulty where it did arise came on that account, and the minority report says that "the Government did nothing in the direction of providing a proper boot for active service, excepting the providing , of a double sole." The evidence of Mr. Matthews, of Ames-Holden-McCready Company, at page 584, is as follows:
Q. I see that this sole also has nails?-A. Yes, hob nails.
Q. Would there be any difficulty in putting these steel slugs and these nai!4 in the sole after manufacture?-A. After manufacture?
Q. Yes?-A. There would be no difficulty in putting in hob nails. Since the investigation was started, the Canadian Government has sent to our factory in -the neighbourhood of 8,000 shoes to be reinforced, or quilted as we call it, in the fore-part and in the heels with nails.



The Government has sent to one factory alone 8,000 pairs to be reinforced or quilted in the sole, which is the most vulnerable part of the boot. I need only draw the attention of the members of the committee to the matter, and they will recognize that there has been a cloud of witnesses who have produced boots that have been quilted in the soles, and that one firm alone has put those improvements in the soles of 8,000 pairs of boots.
Were not those boots sent bach from the Montreal stores?

The evidence does not
show where they came from. Why, in the face of this well-known fact should the minority report say that " nothing has been done by the Government in the way of providing a proper boot'for active service "? Hon. members on the other side of the House may palliate the omission of the minority report to 'commend the vigilance of the department, but no hon. member can excuse the minority for such a palpable misstatement as the one to which I have referred.
The most amazing statement, however, and one which occurs no less than fifteen times in the minority report is that the boots which have been served out to the soldiers "are not active service boots." That is the burden of the song from beginning to end of the minority report. I was much disappointed at the failure of the committee to agree on a report, and it looks to me as though the hon. gentlemen who have submitted the minority report had early made up their minds to bring in an adverse report, which is not founded on the facts disclosed. The minority, after searching the whole record through, find that in their opinion the boot is not an active service boot, and they fasten on this point and reiterate from one end of the report to the other that the boot is not an active, service boot.
It has been pointed out to the House already-and I will repeat it, as it is a matter of importance-that whatever the recognized departmental pattern boot may be, it was adopted in the days when the Minister of War of our hon. friends opposite presided over the Department ot Militia and Defence. Whether the boot came into the department in 1899, 1900, 1905 or 1908, matters not; it was there, an accepted pattern by the department at the time when this Government came into power, and when hon. gentlemen opposite -and it is only they who join in this

minority report-condemn the active service boot, they condemn their own administration of the Department of Militia.
I would have expected my hon. friends opposite to have been more kind to the gallant gentleman who lately presided over that department.
This country has voted large sums of money year after year for the upkeep of. the Department of Militia. In 1897, $1,688,213 was spent; in 1898, $2,500,635; in 1899, $3,624,693; in 1900, $3,106,241; and so on down to the year 1907, $6,795,678; in 1908, $6,408,806; in 1909, $6,921,314, and in 1910, $6,909,211. This money was voted by the representatives of the people, assuming that it was to be spent for the purpose of keeping the permanent force in a state of readiness to defend this country, and engage in serious fighting if necessary.
Did it ever occur to the Canadian people that this money, instead of being spent in equipping the permanent force for active service, was to be spent in holding annual camps where honourary colonels might appear in full uniform once a year without any serious thoughts of fighting in their minds?
We all remember the experiences of our youthful navy, how one-half of it on returning from a junketing trip, ran on the rocks. Do I understand from this minority report that it was deliberately planned by hon. gentlemen opposite and by the late Minister of War that we were to have a toy army as well as a toy navy?
The argument of the hon. member for North Oxford is that this boot is an active service boot suitable for South Africa, but not suitable for France. If that suggestion is followed to its logical conclusion, then Canada should immediately equip itself with a variety of kinds of army boot. She should have one suitable for South Africa; she should have one suitable for France, the country where our men now are: one suitable for work in Belgium, for that is where they will be shortly; we should have one suitable for work, in Germany, for that is where our forces will be soon; and so on ad infinitum; she should have boots suitable for use in every country on which she may at any time wage a war.
It is quite clear from the evidence that a boot very similar to exhibit 12 was worn by soldiers in South Africa. It seems clear that Slater boots were not provided by the department, but soldiers who wanted them had to buy their own boots.
But I should like to show to the House a sample of the real South African army boot, provided by the Administration

under the superintendence of the late Minister of Militia and Defence. There [exhibiting a boot] is a fair specimen of the real boot our soldiers wore in South Africa provided by the department. It is a fair sample-exhibit no. 77.

That is absolutely untrue, and the hon. member knows that. That boot was rejected.
The hon. gentleman says the statement is untrue. That comes as news to me.
