It was this class of
boot, and no quibbling will dispose of that. Furthermore, the present Government are paying $3.85 a pair for boots for our soldiers, and we are told that the Government is not prepared to pay for a good boot; but all that the former Government were prepared to pay for boots for our soldiers going to South Africa was $2.13 a pair. As to the evidence of Mr. McCann, let me follow it a little further, quoting from page 1039:
By the Chairman:
Q. Then those that tame in subsequently were from the same contractor, and were the same kind of boot?-A. Practically the same kind.
Q. And they were for the permanent force and for South Africa.-A. And for South Africa.
Q. And possibly some of them went to South Africa?-A. It is quite possible.
Q. It is quite probable, is it not?-A. I would not like to go that far.
Mr. Macdonald:	The lot of boots of which
this is a sample were all rejected and sent back to the contractor, and therefore this is not evidence.
Hon. Mr. Murphy:	And he said that many
of the men who went to South Africa bought their own boots.

By the Chairman:
Q. Those who did not wore this class of boot? -A. So far as I know, some of them might have gone to South Africa.
By Hon. Mr. Murphy:
Q. Do you know that as a fact?-A. I do not know as a fact; once they were accepted they were returned to the Ordnance Stores.
By the Chairman:
Q. Those who went to South Africa did not buy their own boots, nor this class of boots?- A. It was this kind that went to South Africa.
That settles the question. Where is my hon. friend's charge of misrepresentation now?
I deplore the fact that such an important question, one with which is involved Canadian national and Imperial defence, should be made a party question.
There are, as you know, in the prosecution of a fight, certain rules of civilized warfare; some things are permissible and some are not permissible. Among the acts not permitted in modern warfare is the poisoning of wells. I had sent to me a few days ago-I do not know whether on account of my official position as member of the committee; at any rate it came to me through the mails-a publication called " No. 24." I see that it is published by the Central Information Bureau of the Canadian Liberal Party, Ottawa, 1915. This publication, which bears the official impress of the Liberal party said:
The manufacturers made the shoes that were ordered. If the wrong sort were ordered, the fault lay with the Government, and that is where the fault did lie. They waited three weeks.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the evidence produced by that committee shows that war was declared on the 4th of August. The first business day following the 4th of August was the 5th of August. On the 8th of August, three days later, the Government sent out requisitions to a large number of manufacturers, and on the 10th of August, which was exactly five days after it was possible for them to act, contracts for the manufacture of boots were in the contractors' hands-and still we have from this official bureau that the Government " waited three weeks." I have already declared that we have heard from the pulpit and from the press wild statements with regard to the supply of boots and their quality. I think this little leaflet can properly excuse about one-half of the press of this country from any liability in this matter; this is the quarter from which official information springs for the Liberal party. No fountain can rise higher than its source, and if this is the official infor-
	.
matron-misinformation, distorted information, given out by the central bureau at Ottawa,-it seems to me that the fault lies there with the Liberal party, and not primarily with the press who are supporting it.
The minority report also devotes a paragraph to the middleman:
That in the month of November last the Militia Department directed the Senior Ordnance Officer to purchase boots locally in Winnipeg and 3,798 pairs of boots were purchased there, not directly from manufacturers of boots but through middlemen;
These boots were required for use at Winnipeg, they were purchased at Winnipeg from large wholesale dealers in Winnipeg because there are no manufacturers there, and it does not appear from the evidence produced before the committee that the public interest has suffered in any way whatever. The boots were delivered at Winnipeg at $4 per pair, express paid, delivered free of expense to the Government and the public interest has not suffered. Furthermore, these 3,798 pairs of boots are less than 2-10 per cent of the whole supply of boots ordered since the war broke out.
It is rather significant that the minority report calls attention to the fact that these purchases were made through middlemen and stopped there. Do hon. gentlemen opposite condemn the existence of middlemen, this noxious weed of Liberal growth, or do they hesitate to attack this class whose activities flourished throughout the country in the days of hon. gentlemen opposite? Do they intend to uproot them? It is significant that they call attention to the fact that these middlemen exist and make no recommendation with regard to them.
Our casual research in the department brought us face to face with this institution, fostered-and I say it in all sincerity-by the late Administration. When our search in the department uncovered this institution, it was, in fact, the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) himself who first recognized it. The contract for army boots in 1889 was made with Mr. A. W. Redden, a leading citizen of Halifax, a member of the Legislative Council and a man of the highest standing. He is a stalwart Liberal, of course, else he would not have been called when he was to the " upper chamber " in- Nova Scotia. But Mr. Redden is a retail dealer. The Winnipeg dealers who supplied the boots questioned by the minority are all wholesalers.
The significance of the Redden contract . did not dawn on the majority of the com-

mittee, it remained for the hon. member for Pictou to point it out. The hon. member said (page 1200) :
Mr. Macdonald:	I may state for the benefit
of the committee that Mr. Robert Taylor was one of the people who made that boot with the paper sole that was produced here.
We were content to let the matter rest with Mr. Redden, but the hon. member for Pictou was the means of pointing out that there was a middleman in the transaction.
While it does not appear from our investigation that the public interest has suffered, there is one other circumstance in connection with the supply of army boots which, I think, should not be overlooked. It also is a legacy from bygone days. There was a gentleman well known around the department who formerly was president of the Slater Shoe Company, who dealt largely with the department in the olden days when Sir Frederick Borden presided over that department. In those days it was not fashionable to call for tenders. Mr. Slater was awarded the contract year after year without any call for tenders. The order was simply given out to Mr. Slater. This gentleman ceased his connection with the Slater Shoe Company on January 1, 1913. Within two months he had appealed to the Minister of Militia and Defence for consideration on the false representation that he had become a partner in Louis Gauthier & Co., a manufacturing concern in Quebec. The minister, with his customary good nature, allowed this gentleman an opportunity to tender.

I might say
right here, that no man who is a manufacturer of boots who has ever had his name presented to the Militia Department since I have been there, be he Grit or Tory, reputable or otherwise, but has had his name put on the list and has had the director of contracts search him out to see whether he was fit for the job or not.
Mr. MoCURDY:	The minister's statement brings to my mind other information we found in the committee. We found that the minister had gone to a great deal of pains to ascertain whether this firm should be allowed to tender. Exhaustive reports were at his direction obtained from the mercantile agencies, who reported that this firm of Louis Gauthier & Co., in which Slater claimed to be a partner, was a reputable and reliable firm, well able to carry out a contract if given an opportunity to tender. At any rate, they were subsequently the
lowest tenderers, at $3,724, and as such were awarded the contract for the supply of boots.
My hon. friend has said that the Slater Company got the contract without tendering. What was the price?
I think it was $4.
I understand the highest price was $3.72.

Here is the evidence on . page 903. Charles E. Slater was being examined as regards the Gauthier contract:
Q. Then you ought to have no objection to tell us.-A. Instead of it causing the Government or the Department any more expense, I isaved them money by my connection with Gauthier, and bringing Gauthier into the proposition. In 1913 and 1912 we were paying $4 ,a pair for the boots. That was the year, 1912, when Slater Shoe Co. supplied the boots.
So that on the first Gauthier contract the country was saved 27) cents per pair. It has not been proven by the investigation that the public interest has suffered at all in the matter, but at the same time our investigations disclosed the fact that an abnormal and unfair commission arrangement existed; and although the public interest has not suffered in any way by reason of it, I think the Government, now that its attention had been brought to the matter, can very properly place its stamp of disapproval upon any such arrangement in connection with its business in the future.
It must be very gratifying to all citizens who are anxious for a full and free investigation into the public transactions that the evidence of the committee should, be as it is.
It should also be gratifying to all interested in the fortunes of the soldiers who are so valiantly battling at the front in defence of our common cause, and gratifying as well as to every Canadian interested in the vindication of our great industrial structure, upon whose prosperity depends in turn the prosperity of a large army of employees and skilled mechanics.
In closing, I desire to express the hope that the agencies which have been instrumental in creating uneasiness in the minds of those who have sons or brothers or friends at the front-and that includes all Canadians-and which have been so ready to cast aspersions upon the fair name of one of Canada's great basic industries, may, now that the baseless nature of their charges has been demonstrated, be equally active in removing the false impression which they assisted in creating.

As a member of the committee to which was referred the question as to the character of the boots supplied by the Government to the overseas contingent, I feel it my duty to make a few remarks; and I should like to review very shortly the conditions which existed in regard to this whole matter of the supplying of boots by the Canadian Government not only to the volunteers for overseas service, but to the permanent force as well. We have had some very curious statements and reasoning by some of the hon. gentlemen who, in defence of the rather curious document that has been presented as the majority report, have gone very far afield indeed from the evidence which was presented before the committee. They have discussed almost everything else in the world except the question as to the character of the boots that were given to the soldiers. I might recall the fact that previous to 1899 the number of men permanently engaged in the Militia Force of Canada was comparatively small, amounting to not more than 700 or 800 at the most; and these were scattered at various places over the country at what were known as schools of instruction, where young men who wanted to qualify as Canadian officers proceeded for the purpose of taking a course and receiving their certificates. Previous to 1899, in no one year from Confederation down, was the Militia Department of Canada called on to supply more than 700 or 800 pairs of boots at one time. It will readily be seen, therefore, that the question of the character of boots supplied during that period was not a matter of very serious consequence. It did not engage the attention of the country to a very great degree, for a large number of these men were employed simply as sentries in the quietest kind of way, and had no real part in actual training. When the militia of the country were called out to the camps in summer time the Government of the country at no time, since Confederation down to the present, has ever provided them with boots. Each man provided himself with his own. I thought it well to make these remarks because I am quite sure that a great number of people who have not followed the procedure of the committee, or read the evidence, were under the impression that the Government had in the past been supplying the boots for the militia of this country.
With these premises, let us see where Canada was in 1899 when she decided to participate in the South African war. The
[ Mr. McCurdy.]
result was that the organization of the department, so far as the supplying of boots for any purposes was concerned, was naturally of no consequential character, and from the evidence before us there can be no manner of doubt that the Canadian force that went to South Africa were equipped with boots in this way. In the first place Lord Strathcona sent the Strathcoma Horse and equipped them with everything that attached to a soldier's accoutrements, the department supplying no part of their equipment whatever. It appears that the Van-kleek Hill Boot and Shoe Company supplied the major portion of the boots that were purchased by the Militia Department in 1899 for the mem who went to South Africa.
Did I understand the hon. member to say that the Strathcona Horse were the first that were sent to South Africa?

I did not say who was sent first. I said that the Strathcona Horse were equipped by Lord Strathcona himself. I am speaking of the evidence that is before us, and I do not want my hon. friend the General when his turn comes to speak to bring to the House any data that may be in his department but which was not submitted to the committee. If my hon. friend has any evidence in regard to this or anything else that was before the committee, he should have submitted it to the committee to whom was committed the task of dealing with this question.
I am very much obliged for the lecture. But where was the suggestion that I was suppressing anything?

My hon. friend has shown a disposition to be rather exceptional in his criticism of matters concerning the Strathcona Horse, so I ventured to give him that little suggestion, which I hope he will accept. He is too old a parliamentarian not to accept a suggestion of that kind. The Vankleek Hill Boot and Shoe Company was the one which supplied the boots which went to South Africa. But a great many men who volunteered at that time purchased their own boots. That was given in evidence by some gentlemen Who appeared before us and has been confirmed from various other sources.
I was very much surprised to see the hon. member for Shelburne (Mr. McCurdy), who, all through this inquiry and down to the very last moment of the drafting of this

majority report, was of the opinion that these boots were not suitable for active service, drag into this issue the question of a boot that was produced before the committee and alleged to be a sample of the kind of boot that was sent to South Africa.
I asked Mr. McCann, who is assistant director general of contracts:
Q. Have you got a pattern of that 1,900 South African boot? You have not got a sample boot?-A. X do not think there is one in existence.
And he goes on to say in other parts of his evidence that he had searched in the department and could not find any boot of that kind. Then, as suggested by my hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), his examination proceeds in this way:
By Mr. McCurdy:
Q. Why were the boots rejected if not because they were not according to sample?-A.
I could not tell if it was according to sample or not.	[DOT]
Q. I understand you to say the boots were rejected?-A. Some of them were rejected because they were found like that (pointing to boot). That was not considered a suitable boot to go either to the Permanent Force or to South Africa.
He identifies this particular boot which the hon. member for Shelburne has produced here. The correspondence produced by Mr. McCann will be found at page 1060. It will be found that Mr. A. W. Redden, of the city of Halifax, who was a boot and shoe dealer, and, as it was disclosed afterwards, connected with Robert Taylor & Co., who were boot and shoe manufacturers in the city of Halifax, tendered for the supply of boots for the Permanent Force in that year, and that this boot was one of the samples which had been sent forward in connection with the supply of boots to the Permanent Force, as explained by Mt. McCann at page 1030 of the evidence. The question was asked:
By Mr. Macdonald:
Q. Were there any specifications for that boot at that time?-A. No.
Q. There had been none in the department? -A. No, that was made to sample, and for anything I know to the contrary, the sample may have been made exactly like that.
Q. You say there were 3,000 pairs of boots. What became of those boots?-A. I could not tell you that. You would have to find that out from the ordnance people.
Q. They went to the Ordnance Department, did they?-A. Some of them did and some went to the contractors.
Q. Did you show that to Sir Frederick Borden, the then minister?-A. No, I did not. It was shown to him by the then Deputy Minister.
Q. And what was done in regard to it?-A. The boots were rejected and returned to the contractor, that lot.
Q. What about the 3,000 pairs?-A. I could not tell you off-hand.
Q. They were not returned?-A. Some of those were, returned too.
Then this witness goes on and produces the correspondence which is found at page 1060 and in which you will find that Captain Benoit, director of contracts at that time; wrote to Mr. Redden:
Ottawa, 23rd December, 1899.
A. W. Redden,
Halifax, N.S.
Boots received from you just opened out for inspection. Leather in some, both soles and upper very bad; far inferior to standard and useless for service. Those for South Africa ,niust be of best quality and workmanship. They will be subjected to rigid inspection. Wire explanation fully.
(Sgd.) A. Benoit, Captain.
He had previously written him on the 12th December, 1899, to the following effect:
I now beg leave to inform you that, as the boots will not be required for a second contingent to South Africa, we will have to issue them to our permanent force, who have been wearing a different kind made of brown leather.
On February 13, Captain Benoit, writing to Mr. Redden, says:
Ottawa, February 13, 1900.
Gentlemen,-I beg leave to enclose to you, herewith, a copy of our departmental inspector's report upon 456 pairs of ankle boots we received from you about 15th December last.
You will see from the nature of this report that it was quite impossible that we could accept these boots, 449 pairs, consequently were returned to you on the 2nd instant, via Canada Atlantic and Intercolonial R.R.
The amount of the charges paid for freight to Ottawa from Halifax on the 9 cases of boots -$9.40-will be deducted from any claim you may have against this department for boots accepted from you.
The remaining seven pairs have been kept here for the present for reference.
Among the seven pairs which were kept in the department for reference was found this boot which has been produced here. There was in the filling of this particular boot, according to Mr. McCann, what is known as leatherette. That is what Mr. McCann in his evidence states was in this boot and that was apostrophised by the gentleman who is acting as counsel in this matter as paper and hon. gentlemen have been talking about paper ever since.
The counter was composed of leatherette, but the soles, as the sample will show, were made of ordinary pasteboard from one end to the other.

I speak of the filling. At page 1029 it will be found that Mr. McCann speaks of leatherette as being the

quality of the material used. My hon. friend introduces this matter for the purpose of endeavouring to lead the House and the country to believe that particular boot was one out of a number of boots which had been shown to the committee and that the balance of them had formed part of the boots which had been sent to South Africa.
A similar boot.

A similar boot? Let my hon. friend produce that similar boot. A similar boot has been the refuge of my hon. friend and his friends all through this inquiry. It was not a similar boot. When was this boot supplied?
This boot was supplied.

If my hon. friend had not been so interested in other matters he! would have known that Capt. Benoit stated that the boots were being ordered for the Permanent Force and that this was one of the seven pairs of boots that had been kept out of the 456 that had been received, that the balance were rejected and returned and that none of them got to South Africa. These are the boots (exhibiting a pair of boots) which my hon. friend's friends have supplied the soldiers who have gone to fight the Germans. It will take my hon. friend and his friends a long time to explain ithe shortcomings of this boot without going back into ancient history. If my hon. friend knows anything about Canadian history and about what was done in South Africa he will know that there never was any complaint about the boots which were sent to South Africa during the time when Sir Frederick Borden was Minister of Militia. My hon. friends went hunting in the recesses of the Militia Department and found a boot that was a rejected sample out of 456 boots that were absolutely rejected, which boot happened to remain in the 'department, and the finding of that boot is regarded by these hon. gentlemen as a good and sufficient answer for boots like those which have been supplied to the soldiers to-day. After all his arguments and after all his labouring about that boot, the very best that my hon. friend and his friends could do, when they put their hands to paper is the following to be found at page 585 of the Votes and Proceedings:
The evidence does not justify the committee in coming to the conclusion that with some such improvements as have been suggested the sample boot would not be a good, all round, serviceable Canadian military boot.

Is not that a beautiful commendation- that the evidence does not go so far that it would enable us to come to the conclusion that, with some improvements that have been suggested, the sample boot would not be made a good boot! That is the very best they can say about that boot. The improvements have not been made and the deliverance of the majority of the committee on this whole question is that with some improvements they might possibly make a good boot out of it. I commend to my hon. friend the task of wrestling with the question as to whether he could not do better even than that and not be forced to confess that he was driven to the position of taking up that old boot which was found in the recesses of the Militia Department and discussing it as if it had some relevancy to this question at all.
What happened after 1899? In 1901 the department took up the question of the defence of Canada and from that time on the Militia Department were concerned about the supplying of boots for outfitting the men who were looking after the defence of Canada herself. It became necessary to purchase, instead of 700 pairs of boots a year from 7,000 to 8,000. As a consequence, in 1901, a specification was drawn up. In 1905 the first time, as far as the evidence before us goes, Goodyear welt boots were bought by the Department of Militia and Defence.
Mark you, the boots which went to South Africa were standard screw boots and they were a nailed pattern, and for the first time in 1905 the Goodyear welt was introduced into the department. There is all the difference in the world between these boots, and the battle wages between the two schools of men in the boot world, as to whether the Goodyear welt or the standard screw boot is the better for soldiers. We had in three years 7,000 or 8,000 men in barracks in Canada-at Halifax, London,' Esquimalt, and elsewhere. They were in small groups and their duties were not arduous; in Halifax they manned the citadel and the forts and they were engaged in schools of instruction, and the Militia Department knew very well that in providing two pairs of boots a year for each soldier they were not providing boots which were fit for active service conditions.
As I have said, there is a great deal of difference between the two kinds of boots. A number of soldiers came before the Committee, some from the permanent force and si>me from the expeditionary force, and they explained that they liked to have a

nice dressy boot for ordinary occasions, and one chap who had lived in England said there was no use going up to London with a boot that was not dressy, because he never could get a girl, and that the Canadian boot was good for that, but it was not much good for campaigning. In these years, the Militia Department supplied this boot to the man diving in barracks, when there was no thought of active service conditions. There is no question about that; every member of committee knows it. -Therefore the paramount question which the committee had to consider was. is the boot which was supplied to the men of the overseas force an adequate and a proper boot for active service conditions. These men were not enlisting to do sentry duty or to go on parade in barracks, but to engage in the most serious warfare the world has ever known. The moment the declaration of war was made, it must have become plain to the Department of Militia that above everything else the boys who were going to the front should be equipped in the best possible manner. A man engaged in this arduous duty might have a hole in his. trousers, or the cloth of his coat might toe thin, or there might toe defects in his overcoat; and he could worry along, tout the poor beggar who even in Canada had to train six hours a day, marching through the various evolutions, must have a boot which is comfortable and which will not cause him discomfort and pain. And when you transport him across the ocean and put him up against the task he has to perform in the trenches the absolute necessity for excellence in the character of his footwear becomes imperative. The question for the committee then to consider was, whether or not the boot was a fit boot for active service conditions, and that is the question which the Canadian people want to have answered. If -any hon. gentleman opposite could bring evidence to show that it was an adequate and proper active service boot, then the whole discussion ended. If my hon. friend (Mr. McCurdy) was able to point to one piece of evidence that it was a proper boot for -active service, we need not have this discussion to-night; -but neither he nor any one else has been able to do so. This whole report of the majority of the committee is an absolute apology for -the -boot which somehow or other got under the feet of our soldiers. In legal parlance, hon. gentlemen on the other side have confessed the allegations and they are trying to avoid the consequence by all sorts of suggestions
and learned discussions about the English boot and the American boot, which, of course have no relevancy whatever to the question as to whether or not we supplied our men with the right boot for the purpose it was to he used for. Up to this very moment, no one has come forward to say that this was a proper boot in all respects-. When the Minister of Militia first appeared before the committee he impressed me that he would contend that it was a proper boot for active service, but when I read his evidence carefully, I found he told us very plainly that there was something wrong with the toe, and something wrong with the -heel, and something wrong elsewhere-
Does the hon. gentleman mean to insinuate that I did not state that to the committee? .
State what?
State thait in the opinion of some it should be better at the toe?

I am just saying that you said so. I said that even the Major General did not come to the point of saying that this was an absolutely good hoot for active -service, and that he pointed out certain defects in it.
Not defects.
Inferiorities.
That it might be improved.

The Major General will not speak about this boot in the same sense that some people speak about painting the lily, because he said that this lily boot of his could be painted up, and that if it were fixed in the toe and in the heel and in the instep and in the uppers it would be a first-class boot, but that otherwise it was defective. Practically every man who has had to do with manufacturing these boots has condemned them.
We have heard a great deal about the excellence of Mr. Hoar, from Halifax, as an expert. Hon. gentlemen on- the other side have lauded him and spoken of him as a man who knew what ]he was talking about. He comes from the constituency of the Prime Minister, and he was called by hon. gentlemen on the other side and put forward as a man on whose judgment they were going to rely. Let us see what he says about this boot. He was shown the sample boot, Exhibit 12, which was produced by the department, and he was asked:

Would you consider the sample hoot, Exhibit 12, a fair boot for ordinary conditions, that is the sample by which the Ames-Holden Company were working.
Mark you, this was the sample boot from which Ames-Holden and Company made all their boots, and Mr. Hoar, before he answered the question, was rather cautious, and he said:
Under what conditions? For city wear or what?
Then he was asked:
Would you consider it so under ordinary conditions of military wear?
And his answer was:
Not for campaign work.
Then I quote further from the evidence:
Q. Would you think it was fit for ordinary military work outside of campaign work?-A. Yes, I would.
Q. But for campaign work, you think a different boot should be used?-A. Yes.
Q. What kind of a boot should be used?-A. A heavier boot.
Then Sir James Aikins asked him:
Q. Would you consider this boot fit for country wear?
Country wear, mark you, and the answer of this expert was:
No, sir.
He would not consider the hoot which our boys were to wear in the trenches fit for country wear.
In Canada?

Certainly, in Canada, and he was asked why, and he answered: The sole is not heavy enough." Then he was asked:
What experience have you had in boots for country wear?-A. Country wear?
And he goes on to tell what experience he has had.
Q. Then you would liken country wear to military use. There would be no distinction between country wear and military use?-A. Yes, they would be all right for city wear, but .if the military go into the country they want a heavier boot than this.
It is Mr. Pringle who is asking all these questions.
Q. It is not heavy enough for military purposes?-A. Not for campaigning.
Had the witness ever been on a campaign?
This man stated that he had made military boots in Halifax for military officers and for the men in the garrison all his life.
For thirty years.
Mr. Hoar was the special selection of the bon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. McCurdy), and was brought up here on purpose to say that the sample boot was a good boot.
Not for that purpose. I heard that he was brought here to condemn boots.

My hon. friend was arguing a little while ago in regard to percentages until he got the hon. members present to a point where they could not follow him on the evidence of Mr. Hoar. For my part I want to deal with the whole evidence properly as regards the kernel of the whole matter, which is whether the boot was fit for campaign use or not. Mr. Hoar's evidence is that it is not.
He said that it was a good boot.

That is a great question my hon. friends are always asking witnesses. The witnesses come in and look at the sample boot. It is a pretty boot, just the same kind of boot as every hon. member here wears, but would any of us go far into the woods in the summer time or go marching around the country for five or six hours a day with the boots we wear in the city? Yet that is the sample boot shown. My hon. friends ask the witness: " Is it a good boot?" Answer-" Yes." " Does it look like the other boot?" Answer-" Yes, it looks like the other boot." That is the way in which the thing is done. But I want to go back to the kernel of the whole question, and I make the assertion that there was not a single manufacturer who was asked his opinion about the sample boot who did not condemn it, and that up to this moment no man, including the majority of the committee, has dared to put his signature to a certificate stating that this boot is a good active service boot.
Let us now take the evidence of Mr. J. A. Adams, of the Murray Shoe Company. I will not go into his evidence in detail, but I will call attention shortly to what he says on page 752.
Q. You have -seen boots of the style of Exhibit 12, that has been so much talked of here?-A. Yes.
Q. You did not consider they were suitable for active service, and you submitted a boot

that you thought would be suitable; is that it? -A. Yes, that is it.
This gentleman of the Murray Shoe Company did not think the departmental boot was a suitable one, and he said: " I have a boot that I think is better than this and I will make it, but I do not want to make the other one."
Take Mr. Matthews, of the Ames-Holden-MeCready Company, of Montreal, who was interviewed by the Shoe and Leather Journal last autumn. In his interview he said that this boot, which was being made for the department and which was being given to the soldiers, was not a boot that was fit for active service at all, and that in his opinion this particular boot was a kind of a light boot that they were using in order to get the men accustomed to marching so that they could wear a heavier boot later on. He reiterated that this boot was not one which was suitable for active service.
Take, not Mr. Charles Slater, but Mr. George A. Slater, one of the bubbling, cheerful kind of chaps, who told the department he would not take $20 a pair to make boots like the sample for men who were going out to fight.
Take again Mr. C. A. Sutherland, manager of the Amherst Shoe Company, who supplied some of the boots. What did he do? He supplied these boots to the department in accordance with the sample; but when 125 boys from the county of Cumberland enlisted and were going to the front, he said:	"I have a better boot
for active service "-and he goes to his directors, and his directors with him.make a present of 125. pairs of boots that they have themselves made different from the boots they supplied to the Militia Department, and they say:	That is the boot
that is going to equip the Cumberland county boys." The three hon. members who have seen fit to present the minority report to the House pose as critics, and they point out what might have been done, and what, in their judgment, ought to have been done; but it is well that the House and the country should remember what it meant in a country like this, with no great military organization, to undertake within a period of six weeks after the war broke out, the organization, equipment and despatch of a force of more than 32,000 men. speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

But see what that means. It means this, as was very well pointed out by my honorable friend the member for Brandon (Sir James Aikins). Here were millions of dollars being expended every year for military purposes in Canada. They were expended in the training and drilling of the men, in purchasing big guns, 18 pounders and 13 pounders, in providing rifles, bayonets and ammunition, in purchasing great coats and uniforms and clothing of other kinds as well as boots, caps, and equipment of every kind. These honourable gentlemen, the minority of the committee, have told us in the very first part of their report that one of the. greatest essentials in the equipment of the soldier is the provision of a proper boot in order that his feet may be kept whole and that he can march with ease and comfort. Now they will have us believe that the boots deliberately selected and approved by the late Government, first in 1905 and afterwards considered and again approved in 1910, were not intended for use in war at all; that is to say, the honourable member for Piotou (Mr. Macdonald) desires us to believe-and it is understood that he had aspirations for the position now held

by the Minister of Militia, and, I suppose he must be considered as speaking for the late Administration-that if war broke out, it was -the intention of the late Administration not to put the men into the field at once to fight, but to call a board and ascertain what would be a suitable boot for war conditions and then spend six months or a year in providing them. The first act of mobilization by the late Administration would have been to call a board to provide that which they -say is absolutely necessary for the soldier-a boot for active service conditions. That is the ridiculous position in which the honourable member for Pictou has undertaken to place the late Administration; and I think neither his leader nor the gentleman who held the position of Minister of Militia in the late Administration will be very much obliged to him. Could there be anything much more like comic opera? In the United States the best experts who could be procured in that great country took four years for the purpose of determining what would be the best type of army boot, and the first thing these honourable gentlemen opposite were to do when war broke out, if we are to believe the argument of the honourable member for Pictou, was to call a board- which might take four years to determine the proper type of boot to be recommended. Their next active step in the war would be to let contracts for the purpose of having those boots supplied. According to the argument of the Opposition, the boots which the late Government adopted after much inquiry and consideration were peace boots; they were for soldiers, but they were purely peace boots. Were the soldiers' greatcoats peace coats? Were their guns peace guns? Was their ammunition peace ammunition? Was every part of the equipment of the * soldiers, according to the view of my honourable friend from Pictou, peace equipment? In that case, not only the boots, but the guns and the rifles and the ammunition and everything else would have to be discarded if war broke out, and an entirely new equipment procured for the soldiers.

I was hoping that some worthy gentleman on the other side would have prolonged this debate so that we might have adjourned it until the morrow, as I wanted to speak at considerable 'length; but at this hour of the evening I shall endeavour to condense my remarks to a minimum.
The first I heard of anything wrong in connection with the boots issued to the soldiers of Canada was on my return from the old land towards the latter end of November. Soon after I took occasion to visit one of the centres whence adverse reports had come, St. Johns, Que. I found there about 30 pairs of boot that had been reported by Colonel Gaudeite as being inferior. We examined some that were cut across the soles which to my mind had been burned. Two or three others were worn and. one or two had the outer sole torn off, whether by accident or design I could not say. However, the report had been published in the newspapers that the boots were bad. Any one familiar with the spirit or temper of the Canadian people or any people who have not been accustomed to war under such conditions as have prevailed in Canada ever since the outbreak of war will readily realize the nervous tension affecting the people. Fot instance, a toy balloon crossing over the border near Brockviille set.

the whole community agog, it was an American invasion. A kite flying over Ottawa stampeded the whole city on one or two occasions; and some persons having been heard speaking the German language near Toronto caused a great agitation in that city on an occasion mot very long since. In many ways we have evidence that a certain number of people of the country are more or less readily stampeded, if I may use the term, by these irrelevant matters in connection with the war.
The temper of the people is sensitive at a time like this, and one can readily understand how they would feel at the first whisper that the boots supplied to the soldiers were poor. We had faith in: the great majority of the manufacturers. We believed that they were absolutely honest and square in their dealings. I may say that a great number of them pledged their word that the quality of leather and the workmanship was not only fully up to the standard but above the standard, and that they were turning out a better boot than the contract called for. Almost every manufacturer gave us that pledge. When I heard of complaints, I immediately ordered the boards to report on these boots, and later on appointed a board from my own department to investigate and report. Their report is now before the House. At first it was believed-'and the newspapers took up the agitation-that there was truth in these charges, but as I passed from regiment to regiment and personally investigated, I found that instead of the filling being of jam mixed with cork, as some of the stories had it, the filling was of the highest standard that could be put in boots. It was wax, mixed with cork, which is what the specifications call for. Furthermore, as I went through the country I found very few places where more than a dozen pairs were defective at all, and then it began to dawn on me that there must be something more behind all this, than the good of the soldier or the bad quality of his boots. Every facility the department could afford has been offered to the committee in their investigation; in fact, I had the honour of requesting the first minister to appoint the committee to inquire into the whole question.
I might point out, in connection with my views on the boot question, that some years ago I visited the city of Washington and investigated the American plans of boot making, and what they considered the proper boot for a soldier. It is generally known that the American boot is somewhat lighter

than the so-called Canadian dancing pump. It also has a very broad toe, much too broad to my mind. I purchased a pair once that were supposed to be perfect, but I found that the toe played around inside too much and that the boot was much more uncomfortable than a boot that fitted more snugly. As I told the committee, one of our sample boots exhibited before them would have been better if it had been a trifle broader. I also pointed out that the toes and heels should be nailed, for wearing.
The Canadian boot has stood the wear and tear beyond all expectations. When the troops went to England they were met with adverse weather conditions at Salisbury Plains. The rain poured down day after day, and the men had to wall; around in mud up to the ankles. No boots ever manufactured, whether in England or in Canada, could stand such weather as that. No boots have stood such weather. It is only natural that the Canadian boot, the only ones that were being worn there, should be the only ones to be criticised-at that time the English boot was not being worn by our soldiers. Finally, when the agitation from here reached England, the boys naturally thought: Oh, these boots must really 'be bad. At all events the boots were exchanged fbr English boots, but fortunately for themselves the boys still preserved their Valcartier boots. We have evidence after evidence to show that the British boot has gone clean to pieces. The heavy sole is not proving satisfactory to the English soldier, and to-night in the trenches in France and Belgium the Canadian soldiers are wearing their old Canadian boots, 90 per cent of them having discarded the English boot. The Evening Telegram of Toronto, a paper which cannot be charged with being too friendly to your humble servant, in its issue of February 19, 1915, contains an article from Gorden Dent, one of three brothers at the front. He says:
I guess you have heard about the Canadian boots being no good. Well, they are all right, on my first pair the soles are only worn out and they can be made as good as new. What destroyed them was some of the fellows put them over the stove to dry, which rotted them. The first issue of English boots I happened to get (worse luck) they were fitted to a 2 x 4 plank and there is no support whatever to the arch of .the foot, and the leather is rotten. A complaint was made and they stopped issuing them, and now they have got another kind which are some improvement, but let me halfsole my Canadian boots and hob-nail them and I will out-walk any person who has the English boots.

I have also an extract from a letter from Douglas Jennings to C. A. B. Jennings. It is dated Levington Manor, Wilts, March 9, 1915, and reads as follows:
They have equipped us with those English hoots, steel heels and those great large hoh nails in the bottoms. I am afraid they are going to ruin my feet, for they are very heavy and hard to break in. On pay day I am going to buy myself a pair of boots that I can get some comfort out of, for if I have to do the marches in full marching order that we get I will be a cripple in a very short time.
Here is an extract from a letter written by a soldier on Salisbury Plain to his parents residing in Ottawa:
February 1, 1915.
I notice that the Canadian boots were condemned. Ninety per cent of the men hare cannot wear the English make and want to wear the Canadian boots. I am going to leave the English make behind, and wear the ones from home, as they are more comfortable, although they might not be able to stand as much wear and tear.
A week ago, a soldier who had been invalided from the front, having been wounded by a shrapnel shell, passed through Ottawa on his way to Edmonton. On the way from Montreal to here he showed the folks the boots he had worn at Valcartier and at Salisbury Plain and in the trenches, and which I presume he is wearing in Edmonton to-night. I can also quote an extract from a very distinguished officer at the front. He says: " Our Canadian boots are better than the English. The latter have gone to pieces much worse than the Canadian boots." This bears out Major Currie's statement that the Canadian hoots that stood the wider at Valcartier, but which were discarded by arrangements with the British authorities, have had to be taken up again by the soldiers, 90 per cent of whom are wearing them in the trenches at the present moment.
I shall not take up any more of the time of the House except to point out this. Some of our wagons were discarded. One of the reasons given was that they could not turn in the narrow English roads. I knew that was nonsense, because the Canadian wagon can turn in 31 feet 9 inches, whereas the English wagon takes 35 feet. It was also said that our trucks were not satisfactory at the front, that we had three kinds of trucks. Instead of their having been discarded, however, it turns out now that we are supplying seven kinds of trucks. Our bicycles, which were discarded, have also turned out better than the English, and are now being adopted. Our boots were discarded, and they are 155
now turning out better than the English boots.
In regard to the boots furnished to the Canadian contingent at the time of the South African war the facts are these. The inferior boot which was shown here to-night was the one supplied to the troops but the defects were found in them before they started and a number were returned. A large number of a slightly different make were subsequently purchased and handed out to the troops but the troops would not wear them. The troops, out of their own pockets, largely purchased the Slater shoe and wore them through the South African campaign. It is not correct to say that the Slater shoe was issued to soldiers in South Africa because as a matter of fact it was not. The Slater shoe was bought individually by the soldiers and worn by them through the war. Later on the Slater shoe was adopted by the department and Charles Slater, I think the gentleman's name is, was the 'gentleman who was intrumental in having that shoe adopted. It remained the standard shoe for the department but was remodelled in 1910. In -that year I had the honour of being consulted about the shoe and I gave my views which are very much in favour of a light shoe.
I have always worn -a light shoe and I have always felt that it was much better for . marching purposes. I have never felt any difficulty in wearing a light shoe and I could outmarch men wearing heavy boots. The great trouble with the heavy boot is that unless it is kept well oiled and in a flexible condition it wrinkles and the result is that the soldier wearing it is incapacitated. I prefer a light upper made of flexible leather. If I had my way I would have mercurial tanned leather. As an instance of a light boot I might point t-o wha-t is well known by any one who has studied Highland customs, that the Highland soldier in the olden days, when he was a distinct and superior individual to an even greater degree than he is to-day, wore what one might almost call slippers or shoes very much the same as our running shoes. In my own experience of mountain climbing I have found that the best results come from wearing a sporting or lacrosse shoe. I have no use for the heavy boot. The German and British soldiers wear the heavy boot. The German soldier wears a boot that is much larger than would ordinarily be necessary because he wraps his feet in flannel cloth while the British soldier wears a woollen sock. The French soldier wears a much lighter shoe than the British



or German soldier, the Italian soldier wears a light shoe, the Canadian soldier wears a light shoe and the American soldier wears the lightest shoe of all, some lined and some unlined. The American shoe is lighter than the so-called dancing pump of the^Cana-dian soldier.
I do not wish to detain the House other than to point out that I understood from the right hon. the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that the suspicion of fraud on the part of the manufacturers was the motive for appointing this committee of investigation. As time wore on we found that there was no attempt to show that there had been any fraud on the part of the manufacturers,. and I presume that there was no opportunity of doing so, because there was no evidence of fraud.
The question naturally suggests itself to me: Are these hon. gentlemen doing this for the benefit of the soldiers? Not at all. The soldiers were perfectly content with these boots, and in the Dominion of Canada there are tens of thousands of soldiers wearing them. They were wearing 'them last fall, they have been wearing them all winter, and they are wearing them this spring, and there is no fault to find with the boots. The other day one dear lady came to me in the city of Ottawa, and she said: "It is an awful thing; I saw a poor soldier walking around with his foot actually out of his boot." I said: "That is absolutely impossible." She said: "I saw it myself. There is cloth on his feet." I said: "You must be mistaken; the soldiers are furnished with overshoes in the winter time," and she replied: "Oh, I did not know that." Any one in a snowy country wears overshoes in the winter. We had these overshoes for the men all winter, and they were offered to the men at Salisbury Plain, but they were discarded there because it was thought desirable to supplement the boots with which they were equipped.
This agitation certainly could not have been intended to promote Canadian industry. A gentleman told me that at the time this agitation commenced there were negotiations in progress for a $3,000,000 order for boots for the Russian Government, to be given to Canadian manufacturers, but as soon as this agitation began the order was cancelled and it was transferred to United States firms. This agitation, undertaken for political purposes, was utilized for commercial purposes by rival manufacturers in other countries.

Has the minister evidence in writing of the statement he has

made, and, if so, will he be good enough to submit it to the House?
Submit what to the House?

The Minister stated thjjt as a result of this matter having been brought up-this matter of the quality of these boots which were furnished and for which he claims this side of the House is responsible-
Yes.

-an order for $3,000,000, worth of boots and shoes, which otherwise would have gone to Canadian manufacturers, was transferred to the United States. That is a very important statement to make, and if the minister has any written evidence of it, would he^ submit it to the House? I would ask the minister if he would do so.
Do what?
If he would submit the evidence to the House.
I have submitted the evidence. The honorable gentleman has asked me for the evidence. I have given him my statement. Not a dollar's worth of Canadian boots have been sent to Russia, France-
Oh, yes.
Not to my knowledge.
My honorable friend is mistaken there. We had evidence before the committee that a Montreal firm had a contract for supplying boots to those countries.

Well, I was
not aware of that. I have reason to believe that there would have been millions of dollars' worth sent to this country had this agitation not been carried on.

Let me ask the minister if it is the case that the remark which was attributed to him in the newspapers that the manufacturer who supplied these poor boots ought to be shot could have had some influence upon the Russian Government.

The remark that was attributed to me was that shooting was too good for the manufacturer who made bad boots and furnished them to the soiuiers, but that was after the honourable gentlemen opposite had been instrumental in developing this agitation.
No, it was not.
I made my statement in the middle of January.
That was before the House met.
But the agitation was going on before I came back from England.
It was broadcast among the soldiers, of course.
Not at all; the soldiers were content. This agitation was not carried on for the benefit of the people.
The soldiers started it themselves.

The agitation was not started by the soldiers themselves. It was started in the press of the country and it was not carried on for the upbuilding of the Empire. I have studied the matter from every viewpoint, and no aspect presents itself that can be regarded as having any interest for the people of Canada. This agitation has only been carried on for the benefit of rival manufacturers in other lands and for the benefit of the political party that is now occupying the Opposition and will long continue to occupy that position in this Parliament.
, Mr. PUGSLEY :	Is the minister not
aware that one newspaper that started the agitation in a most active way was that very leading Canadian newspaper in Montreal, the Montreal Star, which cannot be acc'used of favouring the Liberal party?

No matter
how it was started, it was very quickly taken up by our friends opposite. I was pointing out that the soldiers on the other side of Ithe Atlantic, as well as this side, as soon as they saw that the agitation was merely political or commercial, settled down and refused to take any part in it. The soldiers on the other side to a man and the solaiers in the firing line in France, are wearing the soft leather boot in preference to the English hard leather boot. The English hard leather boot has not stood the wear for any two months on an average. In fact, they are issuing hard leather boots to the British soldier and they get an issue every two months or six weeks.
The Canadian boots are better than the English boots; the latter have gone to pieces much worse than have the Canadian
